#+title: Agent skills
#+description: The skill as a construct in agent tooling: the SKILL.md format, its frontmatter, the invocation distinction, progressive disclosure, and how published collections organise their skills. Reference material about a format ORE Studio does not own.
#+type: knowledge
#+level: cross
#+filetags: :external:llm:claude_code:skills:reference:
#+created: 2026-08-26
#+updated: 2026-08-26

* Summary

A *skill* in agent tooling is a document that an assistant loads to
perform a kind of work. Anthropic defines the format for Claude Code:
a directory holding a =SKILL.md= file, whose frontmatter carries a name
and a description, and whose body holds the instructions the assistant
follows. Other agent tools read the same format.

This page records the received notion and the conventions that have
grown around it. ORE Studio does not own the format. For the narrower
definition this project works to, see [[id:87D41A08-0B37-41CE-8483-B59B36BA87FA][The skill in the compass
framework]].

* Detail

** The format

A skill is a directory. It contains a =SKILL.md= file and any supporting
files that file refers to. The frontmatter carries two required fields.
The =name= field gives the identifier a user types. The =description=
field states what the skill does and when to reach for it.

The body holds the instructions. Its length is not fixed by the format,
and published skills range from two lines to several hundred.

** Invocation

Published collections separate skills by who may invoke them. A
*user-invoked* skill runs only when a person types its name. A
*model-invoked* skill may also be reached by the assistant when the task
matches its description. Claude Code expresses the first with a
=disable-model-invocation= flag.

The distinction matters because the description does different work in
each case. For a model-invoked skill the description is the trigger, and
its wording decides how reliably the skill fires. For a user-invoked
skill the description is documentation.

** Progressive disclosure

A skill body sits in the assistant's context whenever the skill runs.
Long bodies therefore cost attention. The common answer is to move
material into sibling files and refer to them from the body, so the
assistant loads them only when it needs them.

The technique has a cost of its own. Material behind a reference is
reached only if the referring sentence is worded well enough to trigger
the read.

** In the literature

The construct has an academic lineage, and the lineage divides.

*** Two lineages

One line stores skills as *executable routines*. Wang and colleagues'
Voyager builds an open-ended embodied agent that accumulates a library
of programs it has written and can retrieve and compose them later. A
skill here is code.

A second line stores skills as *verbal lessons*. Shinn and colleagues'
Reflexion has an agent write down what it learned from a failure and
carry that text into later episodes. Zhao and colleagues' ExpeL
generalises across episodes into experiential rules. A skill here is
prose.

Liu, Ming, Joty and Zhao group all three together as systems that
"store verbal lessons, memories, or routines", and observe that "most
prior methods reuse experience as prompt text or task-specific
routines".

The =SKILL.md= format belongs to the second line. It is prose that an
assistant reads.

#+begin_note
The characterisation of Voyager, Reflexion and ExpeL above is taken from
the related-work section of the paper discussed below. The primary
sources have not been read for this page. Read them before treating this
section as settled.
#+end_note

*** The critique of the textual form

Liu, Ming, Joty and Zhao state the deficiency of the second line
precisely:

#+begin_quote
A textual skill can express what the agent should do in principle, but
not precisely when it should activate inside the policy loop, how it
should alter the next decision, and it is often ignored by the model in
practice.
#+end_quote

They locate the gap as one "between reusable experience expressed in
language and reusable experience that can reliably and explicitly
control agent behavior".

Their example is worth quoting in full, because it names the exact form
this project's stance plane takes:

#+begin_quote
Instead of merely stating a principle such as "avoid repeated searches,"
a PF specifies both when that principle applies and how the next
decision should change.
#+end_quote

*** Program functions

Their proposal is the *program function*, abbreviated PF: "a reusable
state–action intervention function" that, "given the current agent state
and a candidate next action, decides whether intervention is needed and,
if so, explicitly modifies or augments the policy".

A PF exposes two methods. =should_activate= "decides whether the skill
should fire". =intervene= "returns the repair". The returned object
carries one of three types:

- =MODIFY_ACTION= rewrites or refines the next action.
- =INJECT_CONTEXT= appends text the policy sees in its next observation.
- =NOOP= abstains from changing the decision, and still emits an audit
  record.

The design "separates choosing the next action from correcting it: the
policy proposes what to do next, while PFs determine whether the
proposed action should be executed as is, revised into a better action,
or augmented with additional context".

Two implementation details are worth recording. PFs extend =SKILL.md=
rather than replacing it: phase instructions are "declared in the YAML
frontmatter of =SKILL.md=" and attach reminders to named reasoning
phases. And the runtime caps how often a PF may fire, "to prevent
oscillation".

*** Prompt-equivalent skills

The paper defines a precise term for the boundary between the two forms.
A PF is *prompt-equivalent* when both conditions hold: its =intervene=
method emits only =INJECT_CONTEXT=, and the injected text "is a fixed
literal string with no runtime substitution". Such a PF "does nothing
beyond pasting a constant reminder into the next observation", which a
prompt declaration would do equally well.

The distinction is narrower than it first appears. A skill that builds
its injected text from runtime state is *not* prompt-equivalent, because
it adds capability "that no prompt-only declaration can match". Neither
is one that rewrites the action.

The empirical result attached to the term is measured and modest. Adding
prompt-equivalent skills on top of the executable library has an effect
that is "small and mixed across datasets".

** How published collections organise skills

Three public collections show three different organising choices.

The *pstack* collection divides its skills into three kinds. Twenty-one
/principles/ each state one rule. Twenty-two /playbooks/ each give the
steps for a shape of work. The remaining skills are workflow tools. One
skill, a sticky mode, routes work to the others.

The *Matt Pocock* collection divides on invocation. User-invoked skills
are thin and orchestrate; model-invoked skills hold the reusable
discipline. A user-invoked skill may call a model-invoked one, and never
another user-invoked one.

The *Council of High Intelligence* ships one skill and eighteen
subagents. The skill is a coordinator. Each subagent supplies one
analytical lens.

None of the three registers a skill against the kind of artefact it acts
on. Each organises by what the skill /is/, rather than by what it acts
/upon/.

None carries an activation predicate that a runtime can evaluate. Each
relies on the assistant reading a description and judging that it
applies. In the terms above, all three belong to the textual lineage,
and none contains a program function.

One of the three anticipates the finding. The pstack collection includes
a principle named /encode lessons in structure/, whose rule is to
express a recurring correction "as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check,
or script instead of more text". That is the paper's thesis reached
independently by a practitioner. It is also stated as prose advice,
which is the form the paper argues against, so the principle does not
satisfy its own rule.
